AI drug discovery is a crowded field with Recursion Pharmaceuticals, Insilico Medicine and BenevolentAI all selling AI-driven discovery platforms to pharma. Numerion Labs' specific stated difference is its APEX protocol, published with NVIDIA in 2025, which it says screens 10 billion compounds in under 30 seconds on a single GPU.

The product is a deep learning platform, COSMOS and APEX per the company, used to predict which molecules bind a drug target; the AI model is the core product, not a feature layered on top of a database, consistent with what the company describes as its founding as one of the first to commercialize deep neural networks in this field.

A new drug usually starts with finding a small molecule that binds tightly to a specific protein target in the body. The number of chemically possible small molecules is estimated in the billions or more, far too many to synthesize and test in a lab one at a time.

Traditional drug discovery narrows that search with a mix of chemical intuition, known drug families and slow, expensive physical screening. Even with those shortcuts, most candidate molecules that enter testing fail, and the process from target to approved drug can take a decade or more.

Numerion Labs' approach, building on work that traces back to 2012, is to train AI models on the relationship between chemical structure and biological activity, then use those models to predict, before any lab work, which molecules out of a huge chemical space are most worth making and testing for a given target.
